after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=6\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{6} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get]

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{7}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{\sqrt{7}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{(\sqrt{7})}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{7} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{7}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{36} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{7} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola x=6sec⁡t,y=7tan⁡t.

a
x26−y27=1
b
x26−y27=1
c
x236−y27=1
d
x236−y27=1
e
x27−y236=1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter t. We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

  • Isolating the sec⁡t term in the x-equation and squaring, we get

x=6sec⁡tx6=sec⁡tx262=sec2⁡tx236=sec2⁡t.

  • Isolating the tan⁡t term in the y-equation and squaring, we get]

y=7tan⁡ty7=tan⁡ty2(7)2=tan2⁡ty27=tan2⁡t.

Substituting the two equations into the identity tan2⁡t+1=sec2⁡t and rearranging, we get

tan2⁡t+1=sec2⁡ty27+1=x236x236−y27=1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
content.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=6\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =6\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{6} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get]

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{7}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{\sqrt{7}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{(\sqrt{7})}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{7} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{7}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{36} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{36}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{7} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

x=2sec⁡t,y=2tan⁡t.

What is the domain of the parameter t?

a
 t∈(0,π),t≠π2
b
 t∈[−π,−π2)∪(π2,π]
c
t∈(−π2,π2)
d
 t∈(−π,0),t≠−π2
e
 t∈[0,π],t≠π2

decision.explanation: The shown right branch requires x>0, so cos(t)>0. On (−π/2, π/2), sec(t) is positive and tan(t) covers all real values, tracing the entire right branch. The endpoints are excluded because both functions are undefined there.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14064533/assets/90b505954bb714ad86f60e07f7a26c16c954139689d96684ed553a7b494f0527.png)

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$
after.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14064533/assets/b43dcf6c343994e3226e2840a0ae80f60484c8de5d7984f61ec6447185181a76.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0]$ and $[0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get only the right branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the right branch are

$$
x=4\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=7\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$

after.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =9\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{9} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{9}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{81} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{4} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{16}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{81} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{81}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$
